schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch date the war to the latter part of the reign, after chs. 18-19, and wrestle with the obscure third contingent; Ellicott, by transposing a letter, reads 'the Maonites' of Maon on Mount Seir, whom Josephus calls Arabs.

Henry reads the invasion providentially — trouble in the way of duty gives God occasion to show loving-kindness; the confederates were chiefly the children of Lot (Ps. 83), emboldened by Jehoshaphat's tarnished standing after his league with Ahab.
Gill sets the attack 'after' Jehoshaphat's reforms, at the moment he might have looked for peace.
Clarke rejects the received 'other beside the Ammonites' and reads 'some of the Edomites,' following the Targum and the later mention of Mount Seir.

debates.question: Who was the third contingent that marched with Ammon and Moab?

sides.position: some of the Edomites (Mount Seir), following the Targum
the Maonites (Meunim), a distinct tribe of the Seir country
an obscure, uncertain reading not easily reconciled

themes: confederacy of Ammon, Moab, and Seir
corrupted text of the third ally
trouble in the way of duty

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott emend 'from Aram' to 'from Edom,' since the invaders marched round the south of the Dead Sea and no Syrians appear; both place Hazazon-tamar at Engedi (Ain Jidy) on the western shore.
Clarke urges the Edom reading (resh/daleth nearly identical); Wesley keeps 'Syria' as a hint that the invaders came at Syrian instigation to avenge Ramoth-gilead.
Gill takes the reporters for deserters, spies, or borderers who rode in haste to warn the king.

debates.question: Should 'from Aram/Syria' be emended to 'from Edom'?

sides.position: read 'from Edom,' matching the southern march and Mount Seir
retain 'Syria,' hinting at Syrian instigation of the war

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott read 'set himself' as 'put the face' toward a purpose (Dan. 9:3), a fixed resolve; the proclaimed fast is national self-humiliation and an admission of guilt (Judg. 20:26; Joel 2).
Gill grounds the fear not in the enemy's numbers but in the wrath lately announced against Jehoshaphat (2 Chron. 19:2), which he feared was now to be executed.
Clarke: unable to stand against so vast an army, the king sought extraordinary help in an extraordinary way, by a universal fast.

themes: setting the face to seek God

schools.summary: Ellicott glosses 'to ask' as 'to seek' (baqqesh) help from Jehovah and stresses that 'out of all the cities' marks the whole nation; Keil sets the assembly as the frame of the king's prayer before the new court.
Gill: they met not in their several cities but at Jerusalem, at the one house of God.
Henry: the people stood 'as beggars at his door,' meeting where God had promised (2 Chron. 7:15) to hear the prayer made in that place.

themes: the temple as place of prayer
the promise to hear in this house

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil take 'the new court' for the outer court of Solomon (2 Chron. 4:9), perhaps renamed as recently repaired or extended; the king stood facing the people before the court of the priests, echoing Solomon's posture in 2 Chron. 6:12.
Gill sets the king in the court of the people, standing on the brazen scaffold Solomon had made.
Wesley reads 'the house' as the court of the people, the court called new because renewed when the altar was renewed.

Ellicott reads the rhetorical questions affirmatively — God over all kingdoms, none can stand against Him (Ps. 115; 1 Chron. 29:12); Keil lays out the prayer's architecture, from universal sovereignty to Israel's helplessness.
Gill anchors 'God of our fathers' in the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Clarke marvels at the king as 'priest of the people,' offering one of the most elegant prayers of the Old Testament dispensation.

outliers.note: Pauses to praise the prayer itself as 'one of the most sensible, pious, correct, and elegant prayers ever offered under the Old Testament dispensation.'

themes: God in heaven, Ruler of all kingdoms
the covenant God of the fathers

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the clause as appeal to accomplished fact — God drove out the nations and gave the land to Abraham (Gen. 13; 17); 'thy friend' is literally 'thy lover' (Isa. 41:8; Jas. 2:23), preserved in Hebron's name el-Khalil. Keil sets the verse as the first pillar of the plea.
Gill hears in 'our God' a claim of peculiar covenant relation, God as Father to Israel alone.
Wesley reads 'thy friend' covenantally — God bound Himself to be Abraham's friend and the friend of his seed for ever.

themes: the land given to Abraham's seed
pleading from what God has done

schools.summary: Ellicott treats 'a sanctuary for thy name' as a single expression (2 Chron. 6:5-8), the name designating all God is to Israel; Keil ties it to the confident hope voiced at the house's consecration.
Gill reads the dwelling as a long tenure since the land was first given — the ancient occupants now threatened with expulsion.

themes: the sanctuary built for God's name
the house bound up with God's honour
the second pillar of the prayer

schools.summary: Ellicott sees a summary of Solomon's dedication prayer (2 Chron. 6:24-30) and judges 'judgment' (shephot), a noun found nowhere else, a probable ancient gloss; Keil takes the rare word as denoting punitive judgment.
Clarke notes MSS and versions adding 'invoked' — 'thy name is invoked in this house'; Wesley reads 'the sword' as the sword of vengeance, that is, war for sin.
Gill glosses the 'evil' simply as any calamity.

themes: if evil comes we will cry

schools.summary: Ellicott gathers the prohibitions of Deut. 2 and Israel's kinship with Ammon, Moab, and Seir (sons of Lot and Esau); Keil sharpens the irony that the nations Israel once spared now come to expel them.
Gill recalls the ancient charge not to meddle with Ammon, Moab, or Seir when Israel came out of Egypt.

themes: the nations Israel was forbidden to invade
laid before the Judge of all

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'requiting us by coming to drive us out' (Ps. 83), notes 'thy possession' a title of the land found only here, and 'cast' the word of expulsion from Eden (Gen. 3:24); Keil reads it as the hinge of the plea.
Clarke: MSS and Targum make the charge explicit — 'they reward us evil.'
Gill: the reward is 'evil for good,' the inversion of Israel's ancient kindness.
Henry draws a double appeal — ingratitude for old kindness, injustice against ancient rights; those who use their land for God may hope He will secure it.
Ellicott renders 'exercise judgment upon them' (here only) and reads 'our eyes are upon thee' as Judah renouncing all deliberation, its whole thought centred on God's omnipotence (Ps. 25:15; 123:2).

Clarke takes 'wilt thou not judge them' as settled certainty of deserved punishment; Wesley notes the king was surprised before his forces were ready, and that God's justice is the refuge of the wronged.
Gill reads it as a summons to God's tribunal to convict and punish the invaders.
Henry unfolds the upward look as fourfold — an eye of acknowledgment, of faith, of desire, of hope — the sovereign remedy when all is at a loss.
Ellicott reads 'were standing' of the people praying with the king (Ps. 48:9); Keil notes they brought little ones, wives, and sons to pray for deliverance.
Wesley: the little ones were presented before God in distress, to quicken the parents' prayers and to move God to compassion.
Gill sets the people in humble posture toward the most holy place, waiting for the answer.
Henry gives the beggar's plea a voice — 'here are little ones that are innocent' — recalling that Nineveh was spared for its little ones (Jonah 4:11).

themes: all Judah standing before the Lord
the little ones, wives, and children

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil trace Jahaziel's pedigree back five generations to a Mattaniah who should probably be read Nethaniah, a son of Asaph (1 Chron. 25); the Spirit fell on him in the midst of the assembly to promise miraculous help.
Henry marvels at the speed of the answer ('while yet speaking God heard') and at the choice of an obscure Levite singer — 'the Spirit, like the wind, blows where and on whom he listeth.'
Gill sets down the five-generation lineage, anchoring the prophet in a real Levitical house.

themes: a Levite of the sons of Asaph
honour on the ministry of song

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the summons and 'be not afraid' in the line of prophetic encouragement (Isa. 49; 51), and grounds 'the battle is God's' in the title Jehovah Sabaoth and David's word to Goliath (1 Sam. 17:47); Keil glosses it that the Lord will make the war.
Gill hears a rising climax in the address — from the country towns, to Jerusalem, to the king.
Clarke: God will not employ them in the discomfiture; He will take the matter in hand and destroy the host.

themes: the battle is not yours but God's

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil fix the 'ascent of Hazziz' as a pass up from Engedi and the wilderness of Jeruel as the waste table-land now called el Husasah, described from Robinson's survey.
Gill explains 'go down' — the fast forbade marching that day, and Jerusalem stood on high ground.
Wesley: 'go down from Jerusalem,' which stood upon high ground.

Ellicott hears the Red Sea command of Exod. 14:13 and reads 'the LORD with you' as an elliptic promise of His presence (cf. Immanuel, Isa. 7:14); Keil reduces Judah's task to standing and seeing the help of the Lord.
Gill: they shall not need to fight, since the Lord would fight for them.

themes: ye shall not need to fight
stand still and see the salvation

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the deep prostration of king and people 'to do worship to Jehovah' (Lev. 9:24; Josh. 5:14; 1 Chron. 21:16); Keil marks the worship as the pivot to the Levites' praise.
Gill: the king bowed as a token of belief and thankfulness, not mere reverence.
Henry hears in the bow the amen of faith — 'be it unto us according to thy word' — accepting an unseen victory as already given.

themes: worship as the amen of faith

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the Korahites as the leading division of Kohath (1 Chron. 6:22), a minstrel-guild of the first rank remembered in the psalm-headings; Keil carries the praise into the next morning's march.
Gill names them the posterity of Kohath in the line of Korah.
Wesley reads their standing and praising 'on high' as a sign of full assurance of the victory.
Ellicott hears in 'believe, so shall ye be established' the affirmative reversal of Isaiah's warning to Ahaz (Isa. 7:9), and places the march in the wilderness of Tekoa over el Husasah.
Henry: faith was to be their armour — 'that is true courage which faith inspires'; in spiritual conflict too, 'this is the victory, even our faith.'
Wesley takes 'believe his prophets' of Jahaziel's promise and all predictions; Clarke lingers on the Targum's 'believe in the Word,' the Word used personally.
Gill: they rose early, confident and animated by the prophet's word.

themes: the reversal of Isaiah's word to Ahaz
the personal Word of the Targum

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects 'consulted' to 'counselled,' reads 'praise the beauty of holiness' as 'praising in holy apparel' (Levitical vestments), and sets the singers before the armed host as at Jericho (Josh. 6:7); Keil notes the singing was the signal for the ambush.
Henry: singers to charge in the front with nothing to do but praise, by which the king triumphed before the battle — 'praise pleases God better than all burnt offering.'
Wesley echoes the council of war that appointed singers to go before the army, praising the beauty of holiness.
Gill takes the consultation as a conference with the king's officers on the order of the march.

Ellicott presses a wholly natural sequence: a Bedouin raiding-band struck the straggling host, panic spread, Ammon and Moab suspected the Maonites and fell on them, then on each other — a self-destruction like Midian's under Gideon (Judg. 7:22); the prophet foresaw the issue, not the course.
Wesley offers either holy angels in the shape of men or God-raised jealousies; Clarke, following Houbigant and the Targum, reads a chain of mutual slaughter beginning with the men of Seir.
Henry balances hosts of angels or (with Bishop Patrick) their own ambushments, and marks that God struck when His people began to praise — He is never angry at praises.

debates.question: By what means did the LORD's 'ambushments' destroy the confederates?

sides.position: a natural panic and mutual massacre providentially arranged
a chain of ambush and mutual slaughter beginning with Mount Seir

themes: struck at the sound of praise

schools.summary: Ellicott sharpens the vocabulary — 'stood up against' a late idiom (1 Chron. 21:1), 'utterly to slay' the word of the ban, 'helped each against his fellow for destruction' (Ezek. 5:16); Keil follows the carnage from Seir to mutual slaughter.
Gill: Ammon and Moab rose against Seir, supposing them treacherous.
Henry: God makes wicked people instruments of destruction to one another — no alliance can hold those God designs to dash in pieces.

themes: the allies turn on one another
God arms His enemies against themselves

schools.summary: Ellicott fixes the mizpeh/watch-tower (Isa. 21:8) and the sight of dead bodies with none escaped (cf. 2 Kings 19:35); Keil sets the height in the wilderness of Tekoa overlooking Jeruel, the multitude of v.12 fallen.
Gill sets the watch-tower on the cliff of Ziz, for travellers' direction and safety.
Wesley: from the tower on the cliff of Ziz Judah could descry the enemy's numbers, order, and condition.

themes: ye shall not need to fight fulfilled

schools.summary: Ellicott reads 'cattle' for 'among them,' 'until there was no loading' for the abundance, and prefers 'garments' to 'dead bodies'; he crowns it with Joel's type of the judgment in the valley of Jehoshaphat (Joel 3:12). Keil also leans to 'garments.'
Clarke judges 'garments' (begadim) the true reading against 'dead bodies' (pegarim); Wesley explains the wealth by the invaders' confident intent to settle and triumph.
Gill: Judah had only to gather plunder, for the Lord had fought for them.

debates.question: Did Judah strip 'dead bodies' or 'garments' from the fallen?

sides.position: garments (begadim), the reading of many MSS and versions

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott locate the valley of Berachah at the modern Wady Bereikut west of Tekoa (Robinson, Jerome's Caphar Barucha) and note 'unto this day' as an ancient historian's formula (Gen. 28:19; Exod. 17:7).
Wesley and Clarke fix the name as 'valley of blessing / Benediction,' from the praises given God there.
Gill: so named from what they did there.

themes: blessing on the field of rescue
a name fixed in the land

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the return as a festal procession, the LORD having made them rejoice over their enemies (Ezra 6:22); Keil hears the deliverance echoed in the Korahite psalms (46-48) and perhaps Ps. 83 by Jahaziel.
Clarke holds up the king in the forefront as a noble pattern of a leader foremost in devotion.
Gill carries the praise from the valley into the temple.

themes: the king as pattern of praise

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the instruments 'harps, guitars, and clarions' and links the procession to Ps. 47; Keil records the sanctuary destination, the house of prayer become the house of praise.
Gill names the three principal instruments of praise sounding as the host entered the city.
Wesley makes it a call to unwearied, lifelong praise — the earthly rehearsal of an eternal employment.

themes: into the house of the LORD
the place of prayer become the place of praise

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the 'divine dread' on the nations (2 Chron. 17:10; Ps. 48:7) as the proof that the LORD had fought, His warfare seen within a course of events however natural; Keil marks the terror abroad and the rest it bought at home.
Gill: the fear of God fell on the kingdoms whose armies were slain, and on the neighbours besides.
Henry: the neighbours owned 'there is none like the God of Jeshurun' — it is dangerous fighting against those who have God with them.

themes: the fear of God on the nations

schools.summary: Keil grounds the peace in God's gift of rest and marks it as the reign's summing-up (parallel 1 Kings 22:41-51); Ellicott compares the rest of Asa (2 Chron. 14; 15) and of the judges.
Gill: the realm was quiet within and without, none daring to molest it.
Henry unfolds the twofold quiet — a people reconciled to the reformation and a border safe from assault; if God give rest, who can give disturbance?

themes: if God give rest, who can disturb

schools.summary: Ellicott fixes the exact agreement with 1 Kings 22:41-42 (save the Ahab synchronism) — thirty-five at accession, twenty-five years, mother Azubah; Keil notes the one telling divergence to come about the people's hearts.
Gill defers to the parallel record in 1 Kings 22:41.
Henry pronounces the reign's essential character — he did right, kept close to God's worship — while marking the two shadows to come.

Ellicott notes Kings has 'all the way' and a masculine pronoun where the Chronicler has feminine (cf. 2 Chron. 17:3), and renders 'so as to do' the right; Keil reads it as the settled verdict of a good reign.
Henry fills out the commendation — Jehoshaphat did right, kept close to God's worship, and kept his people close to it.

themes: walked in the way of Asa

schools.summary: Ellicott reconciles the notice with 2 Chron. 17:6 — there the high places of heathenism, here the illegal worship of Jehovah; Keil finds the Chronicler's diagnosis in the people's unturned heart.
Clarke: the idolatry was suppressed but some sites left standing, a snare in later reigns; Wesley lays the fault on the people, not the king, in their fondness for ancient custom.
Gill distinguishes the idol high places (removed) from those where the true God was worshipped (left).
Henry: the best magistrates cannot reform a cool people who have not prepared their hearts to serve the God of their fathers.

themes: the high places not taken away
the limit of a king's reform

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the notice beside 1 Kings 22:45 ('how he warred' hinting at this victory), reads 'the words' of Jehu inscribed in the book of the kings of Israel; Keil reads it the same way.
Clarke laments that the book of Jehu is 'totally lost,' though extant when Chronicles was written.
Gill: 'first and last' spans the whole compass of the reign.
Henry identifies the author as Jehu the prophet, who had rebuked the king's alliance with Ahab (2 Chron. 19:2).

Ellicott dates the league to Jehoshaphat's seventeenth or eighteenth year, notes the omitted 'made peace with Israel' and the didactic 'he did very wickedly' implying the alliance was wrong (2 Chron. 19:2); Keil reads the plain notice of the partnership.
Wesley reads it as an aggravated sin, sprung from the family tie and the king's easy temper, punished though only a peaceable matter of trade.
Gill fixes the aggravation — so soon after the prophet's rebuke, and with a king who reigned but two years.
Henry names the old weakness — Jehoshaphat's lingering partiality for the house of Ahab, already sealed by his son's marriage.

Ellicott corrects 'ships to go to Tarshish' to 'ships of Tarshish' (long-voyage vessels), fixes Ezion-geber on the Gulf of Akaba, and weighs whether Tarshish means Spanish Tartessus or an eastern port (cf. 2 Chron. 9:21); Keil reads the plain notice.
Clarke gives the Targum's 'the great sea,' the Mediterranean.
Gill harmonizes the trade with the later refusal to let Ahaziah's servants sail (1 Kings 22:49).
Henry weighs the ingratitude — after victory and wealth, a partnership in commerce with a wicked king.

themes: Ezion-geber and the puzzle of Tarshish

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies Eliezer as otherwise unknown, sets his charge beside Jehu's earlier rebuke (2 Chron. 19:2), and reads 'hath broken' as a prophetic perfect fulfilled by a wrecking gale (Ps. 48:7); Keil reads the plain fulfilment — the ships broken, never reaching Tarshish.
Clarke gives the Targum's 'the Word of the LORD hath broken' the works.
Gill identifies Eliezer of Mareshah, a city of Judah.
Henry draws the double warning of prophet and storm, and the repentance it wrought (the king declined the next voyage, 1 Kings 22:49).

themes: the LORD hath broken thy works
the ships wrecked in the harbour
judgment and mercy from one hand
